messages.subject: What resolution to set MSProcessedImagingExperiment object prior to peakBin
messages.subject_clean: What resolution to set MSProcessedImagingExperiment object prior to peakBin
messages.body_plain:
It's difficult to give a minimum reproducible example with simulated data or a small dataset because there's no exposed constructor available for the MSProcessedImagingExperiment class, nor is it currently possible to modify the raw data <https://github.com/kuwisdelu/Cardinal/issues/14> of a MSProcessedImagingExperiment object (e.g., as generated by as(Cardinal::simulateImage(preset = 1, npeaks = 10, nruns = 1, baseline=1), "MSProcessedImagingExperiment")).

Consequently, I describe my experience on a small subset of a real dataset stored in imzML format. Reproducible code and data can be found in this Google Colab notebook (running R version 4.0.1): https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1X5ISmAUpjDLegdQsW0UcjC_aBnJbbbnS. Please see the Colab notebook for the full example. Below is just a brief summary.

Assume we have a MSProcessedImagingExperiment object named mse. The problem is that peakBin() appears to operate on the sparse intensity matrix (e.g., as given by spectra(mse)), which is binned on-the-fly according to resolution(mse). However, since peakBin() operates independently on each pixel, would it not be more appropriate to bin based on the raw data, e.g., as given by intensityData(mse) or peakData(mse), rather than the on-the-fly binned intensity matrix? Thus, my specific question are as follows:
How is on-the-fly binning performed? How is the sparse matrix spectra(mse) re-generated or re-computed each time resolution(mse) is changed?
Is it possible to run peakBin() on the raw data as given by intensityData(mse) or peakData(mse), rather than the on-the-fly binned intensity matrix?
If not, what on-the-fly resolution should be used? Conceptually, it seems like it shouldn't hurt to set resolution(mse) to a smaller (i.e., more precise) ppm value than the instrument's actual precision, since it's the tolerance argument of peakBin() that controls how the m/z values are actually binned. Is this a correct understanding? For context, we estimate the actual instrument resolution to be ~5 ppm, and Cardinal estimates ~3 ppm from the data itself.
Thanks in advance for your help.

Hi Frédéric,

If you look at the pixel count the subset pulls out the ROI you specified. You can set a new run name by assigning it to like so:
run(dataset) <- as.factor('new_run_name')

But as far as I know, there is no function to do so automatically right now.

I've written a function called updateMetadata in my own small package that takes the Spot List exported from flexImaging (File > Export > Spot List) and a .csv file you can make yourself (example in the data folder of my repo).

https://github.com/gtluu/cardinalscripts

The name of each ROI as seen in flexImaging is defined in the .csv file along with the condition(s). The Spot File provides the x-y coordinates for each ROI, and a new column in pixelData() is made for each condition. Here is an example:

 <https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fi.imgur.com%2FgEznCD9.png&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNFqs1zxoJKDi9NpnChECJoJOBF5ew>
In this example you can run:
meansTest(x, ~ condition, groups=pixelData(x)$run)

Hope this helps!

- Gordon

messages.subject: Re: What resolution to set MSProcessedImagingExperiment object prior to peakBin
messages.subject_clean: What resolution to set MSProcessedImagingExperiment object prior to peakBin
messages.body_plain:
Hi Benjamin,

these are important questions, I can answer parts of them:

To my understanding the on the fly binning works similar to peakBin. Therefore, I would suggest instead of reading the file (1st binning) and then bin it with peakBin (2nd binning), to directly use the on the fly binning while reading the data to bin the underlying raw data. e.g. if you want to bin to 10ppm, just read the data with 1ppm resolution, then no further binning should be required.

Regarding question 3: generally yes, but depends on what you plan to do with the data. If you later bin or align the data, you should read it in with smaller resolution and in the step of binning/alignment apply the actual precision of the MS. But in case you want to perform peak picking between reading and binning/alignment be careful not to use a too small resolution for reading the data as this could split up your peaks into several ones. This can be controlled with the plot() function on a small m/z range that contains a known peak. If your only processing consists of binning and TIC normalization, you could read the data with the precision of the instrument (instead of peakBin) and then perform TIC.

I hope that helps a bit.
Best,
Melanie

messages.subject: Re: What resolution to set MSProcessedImagingExperiment object prior to peakBin
messages.subject_clean: What resolution to set MSProcessedImagingExperiment object prior to peakBin
messages.body_plain:
1. Yes, for MSProcessedImagingExperiment, the spectra(mse) matrix is re-computed on-access based on resolution(mse).

2. Currently, all pre-processing operates on the spectra(mse) matrix so that the same pre-processing methods can be used regardless of the underlying data representation (i.e., for both "continuous" and "processed" imzML). I agree that it would be desirable to use the underlying data. This would require some internal re-design.

3a. Because the resolution(mse) is interpreted as a bin width, it can cause problems if it implies smaller increments than the actual underlying data. The issue is that using smaller bins than the actual difference between consecutive m/z measurements can cause "gaps" in the peaks. So the resolution(mse) should actually be set as closely as possible to the actual difference in consecutive m/z measurements in the data as possible, which is what Cardinal tries to estimate as the "resolution".

3b. The tolerance argument of peakBin() does not set the bin size--it sets the tolerance for how local maxima are matched to reference peaks. This is the difference between peakBin() and mzBin(). For peakBin(), local maxima in each spectra are matched to a set of reference peaks, and then the peak is expanded to its boundaries (local minima on either side of the peak). Then either the maximum height or the area of the peak is returned. The tolerance does not affect the bin width in this case, only how distant a local maxima can be when being matched to the reference peaks. (If there are no local maxima within the tolerance of the reference peak, then 0 is returned for that peak.)

-Kylie

messages.body_plain:
Because of how run() and coord() are handled differently in a PostionDataFrame, you cannot do a straightforward join.

I'd say you have the right idea--converting to a ordinary data.frame (or tibble), and then converting back to a PositionDataFrame.

I'll note that there is some fragility in your approach in that it assumes the names of the run and coordinate columns, which are not actually guaranteed (and why they are typically accessed via accessor functions). While "run", "x", "y" are usually a safe assumption, this isn't 100% guaranteed to work. This shouldn't be a problem if used primarily on your own datasets/code.

I'll also note that DataFrame (from which PositionDataFrame extends) is more permissive in its columns than a tibble. The dplyr functions will fail on some data frames with S4 columns (which is part of why they were deprecated in Cardinal 2.6). Again, this isn't a problem if you're primarily using it on your own datasets/code.

-Kylie

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I have a student who is trying to verify certain features in her data. She would like to see if there is fragmentation data for the peak(s) of interest. She acquired this data on a Waters-TOF and was supplied extremely large data files. I tried to use readMSIdata for one of her ibd files (6GB) and it just ran, and ran, and ran, so I finally ended the R session. I guess what I would like to ask, is it possible to just extract the MS data and verify that a fragment ion comes from a feature. I understand that a better option would be to run an LC-MSMS experiment for verification, but this is the data she has.

Thank you for your time and any help you can supply!

messages.body_plain:
Given that it is taking some time for read the data, I would assume the files are "processed" imzML, so Cardinal is reading the full dataset to infer the mass range and an appropriate binning resolution. You can bypass this by setting the mass.range and resolution parameters.

Once imported, the binned mass spectra are available as the columns of the spectra() matrix, and the raw ibd data is available using the peakData() accessor.

You can plot images for particular ions with image(), but I would advise pre-processing the data first or the images will take some time to compile from the ibd file (which is optimized for loading spectra rather than images).

Currently, Cardinal does not do any feature identification or provide access to any databases, so you or your student would have to know the m/z of the ions you're looking for.

-Kylie
